claims.evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of the valence detection task data.

claims.claim: Increased sensory noise (motion variance) rendered motion discrimination more difficult, slowing reaction times.
claims.source: Replicating previous results (de Gardelle and Summerfield, 2011; Spence et al., 2016), increased sensory noise (motion variance) rendered motion discrimination more difficult, slowing reaction times (median RT, main effect Variance, F(1,24) = 4.76, p=0.039, partial η2 = 0.17,) and decreasing sensitivity (d', main effect Variance, F(1, 24) = 185.15, p<0.001, partial η2 = 0.89, see Figure 2B,i).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of the experimental data that replicates previous studies.

claims.claim: Increased sensory noise (motion variance) decreased sensitivity (d').
claims.source: Replicating previous results (de Gardelle and Summerfield, 2011; Spence et al., 2016), increased sensory noise (motion variance) rendered motion discrimination more difficult, slowing reaction times (median RT, main effect Variance, F(1,24) = 4.76, p=0.039, partial η2 = 0.17,) and decreasing sensitivity (d', main effect Variance, F(1, 24) = 185.15, p<0.001, partial η2 = 0.89, see Figure 2B,i).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of the experimental data that replicates previous studies.

claims.claim: Participants were generally unbiased in their tendency to respond left or right across conditions.
claims.source: Although participants were generally unbiased in their tendency to respond left or right across conditions (choice criterion (c), grand mean F(1, 24) = 1.45, p=0.24), a variance × cue interaction was found such that c was increased on low variance disgust-cued trials, but reduced on high variance disgust-cued trials (V × P interaction, F(1, 24) = 10.46, p=0.004, partial η2 = 0.30).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claims.claim: A variance × cue interaction was found such that choice criterion was increased on low variance disgust-cued trials, but reduced on high variance disgust-cued trials.
claims.source: Although participants were generally unbiased in their tendency to respond left or right across conditions (choice criterion (c), grand mean F(1, 24) = 1.45, p=0.24), a variance × cue interaction was found such that c was increased on low variance disgust-cued trials, but reduced on high variance disgust-cued trials (V × P interaction, F(1, 24) = 10.46, p=0.004, partial η2 = 0.30).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claims.claim: On trials following neutral cues, choice criterion did not differ between noise levels.
claims.source: Follow-up paired-samples t-tests on this effect revealed that on trials following neutral cues, c did not differ between noise levels (CB NH – NL; t(24) = 0.26, p=0.80), whereas disgust cues increased rightward bias for low variance trials (CB DH – DL t(24) = 3.76, p<0.001).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claims.claim: Disgust cues increased rightward bias for low variance trials.
claims.source: Follow-up paired-samples t-tests on this effect revealed that on trials following neutral cues, c did not differ between noise levels (CB NH – NL; t(24) = 0.26, p=0.80), whereas disgust cues increased rightward bias for low variance trials (CB DH – DL t(24) = 3.76, p<0.001).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claims.claim: Unseen, arousing cues selectively increased biases for low noise (high precision) stimuli, in the absence of any differences in the speed or accuracy of motion discrimination.
claims.source: These results demonstrate that unseen, arousing cues selectively increased biases for low noise (high precision) stimuli, in the absence of any differences in the speed or accuracy of motion discrimination.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the statistical findings.

claims.claim: An M-Ratio (m'/d') of one indicates optimal metacognitive sensitivity.
claims.source: According to SDT, an M-Ratio (m'/d') of one indicates optimal metacognitive sensitivity (i.e., confidence ratings exhaust sensory information), with lower ratios indicating poorer metacognition.
claims.evidence: This describes a principle of signal detection theory.

claims.claim: The M-Bias parameter describes the amount of sensory evidence needed to report a particular level of confidence, with higher values indicating a higher overall subjective uncertainty.
claims.source: Alternatively, the M-Bias parameter describes the amount of sensory evidence needed to report a particular level of confidence, with higher values indicating a higher overall subjective uncertainty (i.e., a more conservative confidence bias).
claims.evidence: This describes a principle of signal detection theory.

claims.claim: Arousing disgust cues counter-acted the conservative bias induced by high sensory noise.
claims.source: Consistent with interoceptive inference, we found that arousing disgust cues counter-acted the conservative bias induced by high sensory noise (F(1, 24) = 6.19, p=0.020, partial η2 = 0.21), see Figure 2C,iv.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claims.claim: Following neutral cues, confidence reports were significantly more conservative for noisy stimuli.
claims.source: Following neutral cues, confidence reports were significantly more conservative for noisy stimuli (MB NH – NL; t(24) = 2.25, p=0.034), reproducing the previously reported impact of stimulus noise on uncertainty (Spence et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis that replicates previous research.

claims.claim: Disgust cues reduced the effect of noise on confidence, decreasing uncertainty for high variance trials and increasing it for low-variance trials.
claims.source: In contrast, disgust cues reduced this effect, decreasing uncertainty for high variance trials and increasing it for low-variance trials (MB DH – DL; t(24) = −0.197, p=0.85).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claims.claim: Cues did not disrupt or alter metacognitive sensitivity.
claims.source: Indeed, cues did not disrupt or alter metacognitive sensitivity; no significant effects were found for M-Ratio (all p>0.6).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claims.claim: Overall M-Ratio and M-Bias did not correlate significantly with one another.
claims.source: Additionally, overall M-Ratio and M-Bias did not correlate significantly with one another (r = 0.37, p=0.07).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claims.claim: Perceptual and metacognitive biases for noisy stimuli are selectively altered by arousing disgust cues, even in the absence of performance differences in perception or metacognition.
claims.source: These results demonstrate that perceptual and metacognitive biases for noisy stimuli are selectively altered by arousing disgust cues, even in the absence of performance differences in perception or metacognition.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the statistical findings.

claims.claim: The grand mean pupil response shows a canonical orientation response locked to trial onset.
claims.source: Inspection of the grand mean response for each measure revealed a canonical orientation response locked to trial onset (i.e., the forward mask), as characterized by pupillary dilation (grand mean peak at 2110 ms post-baseline, Figure 3A) and heart rate deceleration (grand mean trough at 1900 ms post-baseline, Figure 4A) (Sokolov, 1963; Graham and Clifton, 1966).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from physiological data analysis supported by cited references.

claims.claim: The grand mean cardiac response shows a canonical orientation response characterized by heart rate deceleration.
claims.source: Inspection of the grand mean response for each measure revealed a canonical orientation response locked to trial onset (i.e., the forward mask), as characterized by pupillary dilation (grand mean peak at 2110 ms post-baseline, Figure 3A) and heart rate deceleration (grand mean trough at 1900 ms post-baseline, Figure 4A) (Sokolov, 1963; Graham and Clifton, 1966).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from physiological data analysis supported by cited references.

claims.claim: Sensory noise increased pupil dilation.
claims.source: Consistent with its impact on discrimination difficulty, sensory noise increased pupil dilation (peak effect = 2121 ms post-baseline, duration 554–2377 ms, max β = 24.74, cluster p=0.014) (Kahneman and Beatty, 1966; Murphy et al., 2014b).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from physiological data analysis supported by cited references.

claims.claim: Confidence showed a biphasic relationship with pupil dilation depending on trial time, marked by greater dilation during stimulus presentation but increased constriction during confidence rating.
claims.source: Confidence showed a biphasic relationship with dilation depending on trial time, marked by greater dilation during stimulus presentation (peak dilation effect = 712 ms post-baseline (pb), max β = 11.35, Minimum Cluster p=0.038, duration 676–1560 ms post-baseline), but increased constriction during confidence rating (peak constriction effect = 2273 ms post-baseline, max β = −18.53, Minimum Cluster p=0.038, duration 676–1560 ms post-baseline), see Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from physiological data analysis.

claims.claim: Unseen disgust cues significantly increased both pupil dilation and cardiac acceleration.
claims.source: Confirming that our manipulation successfully modulated arousal, unseen disgust cues significantly increased both pupil dilation and cardiac acceleration (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, and Figure 4c), with increased pupil dilation during motion choice (peak at 1596 ms post stimulus, duration 1686–2403 ms, max β = 21.85, cluster p=0.032) and greater cardiac acceleration during confidence ratings (peak effect 3200 ms, duration = 2900–3700 ms, max β = 0.31, cluster p=0.044).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from physiological data analysis.

claims.claim: Confidence was related to heart-rate acceleration throughout the trial, with greater confidence linked to a faster heart rate in the interval lasting from stimulus presentation to ratings.
claims.source: Confidence was also related to heart-rate acceleration throughout the trial, with greater confidence linked to a faster heart rate in the interval lasting from stimulus presentation to ratings (peak effects at 500 ms and 3900 ms, durations 100–1000 ms and 1600–4100 ms, max β = 0.31, cluster Ps = 0.046 and 0.002), see Figure 4A.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from physiological data analysis.

claims.claim: Pupillary fluctuations encode the interaction of exteroceptive noise and unexpected internal arousal, time locked to the response interval and onset of confidence rating.
claims.source: Pupil responses also encoded the interaction of cue and motion variance in the same time interval as the overall cue main effect, with cues reversing the dilatory effect of sensory noise (peak effect 1467 ms post-baseline, duration 1492–2472 ms, min β = −21.67, cluster p=0.034, Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from physiological data analysis.

claims.claim: The cue-induced reversal of pupillary noise encoding was related to confidence in a positive three-way interaction.
claims.source: Crucially, this effect was related to confidence in a positive three-way interaction (peak effect 1512 ms post-baseline, duration 683–2099 ms, max β = 21.22, cluster p=0.008, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), demonstrating that trial-by-trial fluctuations in subjective confidence tracked the cue-induced reversal of pupillary noise encoding.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from physiological data analysis.

claims.claim: Trial-by-trial fluctuations in subjective confidence tracked the cue-induced reversal of pupillary noise encoding.
claims.source: Crucially, this effect was related to confidence in a positive three-way interaction (peak effect 1512 ms post-baseline, duration 683–2099 ms, max β = 21.22, cluster p=0.008, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), demonstrating that trial-by-trial fluctuations in subjective confidence tracked the cue-induced reversal of pupillary noise encoding.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the physiological data analysis.

claims.claim: The impact of disgust cue on confidence biases relates to a shift in the mapping between noise-induced uncertainty and physiological responses.
claims.source: This finding mirrors our primary behavioural effect, indicating that the impact of disgust cue on confidence biases relates to a shift in the mapping between noise-induced uncertainty and physiological responses.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claims.claim: Cardiac signals were insensitive to sensory noise or noise by cue interactions.
claims.source: In contrast, cardiac signals were insensitive to sensory noise or noise by cue interactions.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from physiological data analysis.

claims.claim: The magnitude of the cue-related cardiac main effect negatively interacted with confidence.
claims.source: Instead, the magnitude of the cue-related cardiac main effect negatively interacted with confidence (peak effect 2800 ms post-baseline, duration 2800–3200 ms, min β = −0.30, cluster p=0.044), supporting a reversal in the mapping between heart rate acceleration and subjective uncertainty (Figure 4C,D).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from physiological data analysis.

claims.claim: Experimentally induced increases in arousal disrupt the typical relationship of heart-rate acceleration and confidence.
claims.source: This latter effect demonstrates that experimentally induced increases in arousal disrupt the typical relationship of heart-rate acceleration and confidence.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the physiological data analysis.

claims.claim: Unexpected arousal regulates the influence of sensory precision on perceptual uncertainty.
claims.source: Our results demonstrate that unexpected arousal regulates the influence of sensory precision on perceptual uncertainty.
claims.evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on the experimental findings.

claims.claim: The integration of expected internal state and the precision of sensory inputs is consistent with an interoceptive inference mechanism.
claims.source: This integration of expected internal state and the precision of sensory inputs is consistent with an interoceptive inference mechanism (Seth, 2013; Barrett and Simmons, 2015), and strongly supports a role for decision-independent sources in guiding confidence.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings, supported by cited theoretical frameworks.

claims.claim: The study strongly supports a role for decision-independent sources in guiding confidence.
claims.source: This integration of expected internal state and the precision of sensory inputs is consistent with an interoceptive inference mechanism (Seth, 2013; Barrett and Simmons, 2015), and strongly supports a role for decision-independent sources in guiding confidence.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claims.claim: The study demonstrates consistent correlations of trial-by-trial confidence with interoceptive arousal, as indexed by both cardiac acceleration and pupil dilation.
claims.source: In general, we demonstrate consistent correlations of trial-by-trial confidence with interoceptive arousal, as indexed by both cardiac acceleration and pupil dilation.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of findings from the study.

claims.claim: Pupil dilation covaried biphasically with subjective confidence, reversing from positive to negative during subjective ratings.
claims.source: In contrast to the linear positive correlation observed for cardiac acceleration, pupil dilation covaried biphasically with subjective confidence, reversing from positive to negative during subjective ratings (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the physiological data analysis.

claims.claim: The biphasic pupil-confidence relationship may partially account for findings that distinct stimulus-related and post-decisional computations underlie the representation of confidence.
claims.source: This result may partially account for recent findings that distinct stimulus-related and post-decisional computations underlie the representation of confidence (Lebreton et al., 2015; Rahnev et al., 2015), and corroborates the previously reported link between pupil variability and confidence for an auditory discrimination task (Lempert et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation linking the current findings to previous research.

claims.claim: The study corroborates the previously reported link between pupil variability and confidence for an auditory discrimination task.
claims.source: This result may partially account for recent findings that distinct stimulus-related and post-decisional computations underlie the representation of confidence (Lebreton et al., 2015; Rahnev et al., 2015), and corroborates the previously reported link between pupil variability and confidence for an auditory discrimination task (Lempert et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This relates the current findings to a cited previous study.

claims.claim: This study is the first to show that confidence reports for perception correlate positively with cardiac acceleration.
claims.source: Furthermore, although interoceptive (i.e., cardiac) sensitivity and meta-cognition for memory have previously been related to one another (Garfinkel et al., 2013), our study is the first to show that confidence reports for perception correlate positively with cardiac acceleration.
claims.evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study's findings.

claims.claim: The results demonstrate a close link between perceptual confidence and interoceptive arousal, even when accounting for decision difficulty.
claims.source: These results thus demonstrate a close link between perceptual confidence and interoceptive arousal, even when accounting for decision difficulty.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claims.claim: Disgust cues evoked task-orthogonal, unpredictable increases in both cardiac and pupillary responses.
claims.source: Our disgust cues evoked task-orthogonal, unpredictable increases in both cardiac and pupillary responses.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the physiological data analysis.

claims.claim: Arousal prediction errors counter-acted the influence of sensory noise on confidence.
claims.source: These 'arousal prediction errors' (APEs) counter-acted the influence of sensory noise on confidence, supporting the recent proposal that interoceptive inference weights the confidence or precision of exteroceptive sensory signals (Seth, 2013; Barrett and Simmons, 2015; Chanes and Barrett, 2016).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings, supported by cited theoretical frameworks.

claims.claim: The mechanism of arousal prediction errors weighting sensory precision was evident in pupillary signals, where the impact of cues on the encoding of sensory noise correlated with trial-by-trial confidence.
claims.source: This mechanism was also evident in pupillary signals, where the impact of cues on the encoding of sensory noise correlated with trial-by-trial confidence.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the physiological data analysis.

claims.claim: Pupil dilation has previously been shown to relate to the overall gain or representational stability of the cortical hierarchy.
claims.source: Pupil dilation has previously been shown to relate to the overall gain or representational stability of the cortical hierarchy (Servan-Schreiber et al., 1990; Eldar et al., 2013; Cheadle et al., 2014; for review, see Hauser et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claims.claim: The results corroborate the proposal that pupil variability indexes the impact of unexpected arousal on perceptual precision.
claims.source: Our results corroborate this proposal, suggesting that pupil variability indexes the impact of unexpected arousal on perceptual precision.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings in relation to previous research.

claims.claim: While cues shifted the relative mapping of heart rate and confidence, no influence of sensory noise on the heart was observed.
claims.source: In contrast, while cues also shifted the relative mapping of heart rate and confidence, we did not observe an influence of sensory noise on the heart.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the physiological data analysis.

claims.claim: The cardiac effects may simply be downstream of cue-induced central nervous system arousal.
claims.source: This may reflect either an issue of causality – our cardiac effects may simply be downstream of cue-induced central nervous system arousal – or it may reflect a more specific encoding of interoceptive but not exteroceptive certainty.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claims.claim: The cardiac effects may reflect a more specific encoding of interoceptive but not exteroceptive certainty.
claims.source: This may reflect either an issue of causality – our cardiac effects may simply be downstream of cue-induced central nervous system arousal – or it may reflect a more specific encoding of interoceptive but not exteroceptive certainty.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claims.claim: The results are difficult to accommodate within feed-forward observer models, which posit that confidence depends solely on the information determining stimulus detection.
claims.source: Because our manipulation of arousal was by design independent from discrimination accuracy, these results are difficult to accommodate within feed-forward observer models, which posit that confidence depends solely on the information determining stimulus detection (Galvin et al., 2003; Lau and Rosenthal, 2011; Maniscalco and Lau, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in relation to existing theoretical models.

claims.claim: Arousal might alter the overall rate of evidence accumulation or the decision threshold.
claims.source: For example, one possibility is that arousal alters the overall rate of evidence accumulation or the decision threshold (Kiani and Shadlen, 2009; Vinck et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative alternative explanation supported by cited references.

claims.claim: On an evidence accumulation model, arousal would increase confidence by offsetting the overall impact of sensory noise.
claims.source: On this model, arousal would increase confidence by offsetting the overall impact of sensory noise.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative prediction based on an alternative theoretical model.

claims.claim: A dynamic or two-stage model could potentially account for decision-independent reductions in confidence if arousal linearly shifts the confidence criterion.
claims.source: Similarly, a dynamic or two-stage model could potentially account for decision-independent reductions in confidence (Pleskac and Busemeyer, 2010), if arousal linearly shifts the confidence criterion.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative alternative explanation supported by a cited reference.

claims.claim: Neither evidence accumulation nor two-stage models would predict the nonlinear interaction of unexpected arousal and confidence observed in the study.
claims.source: However, neither model would predict the nonlinear interaction of unexpected arousal and confidence observed here.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of alternative models in explaining the findings.

claims.claim: Disgust cues seemed to enhance a slight rightward bias for high precision stimuli.
claims.source: Interestingly, we also observed an interaction between cue valence and sensory noise for participant response bias. Although all participants were right handed, disgust cues seemed to enhance a slight rightward bias for high precision stimuli.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral data analysis.

claims.claim: The response bias result may point to a role for unconscious arousal in strengthening the influence of priors on perceptual inference.
claims.source: This result may point to a role for unconscious arousal in strengthening the influence of priors on perceptual inference.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the response bias finding.

claims.claim: The prevalence for participants to engage in the 'gambler's fallacy' is well documented.
claims.source: Although motion directions were presented randomly across trials, the prevalence for participants to engage in the 'gambler's fallacy', in which a 'streak' of repeated outcomes leads to increased belief that this outcome is more likely, is well documented (Tversky and Kahneman, 1971, 1974).
claims.evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claims.claim: By boosting the precision of pre-stimulus beliefs, participants come to believe that stimuli following arousing cues will conform to their erroneous motion expectations.
claims.source: The suggestion here is that by boosting the precision of pre-stimulus beliefs (i.e., expected precision), participants come to believe that stimuli following arousing cues will conform to their (erroneous) motion expectations.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the response bias finding.

claims.claim: This interpretation is consistent with the more general role of expected precision in bottom-up and top-down attention.
claims.source: This interpretation is consistent with the more general role of expected precision in bottom-up and top-down attention (Feldman and Friston, 2010).
claims.evidence: This relates the interpretation to existing theoretical frameworks supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Neurobiologically, expected precision (or volatility) is implemented through gain control by neuromodulation, as regulated by insular, cingulate, pulvinar and other limbic areas rich in neuromodulatory neurons.
claims.source: Neurobiologically, expected precision (or volatility) is implemented through gain control by neuromodulation, as regulated by insular, cingulate, pulvinar and other limbic areas rich in neuromodulatory neurons (Friston et al., 2012; Moran et al., 2013; Schwartenbeck et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claims.claim: Active inference models suggest that the regulation of expected precision is a central mechanism underlying both bottom-up (i.e., salience) and top-down attention.
claims.source: Active inference models suggest that the regulation of expected precision is a central mechanism underlying both bottom-up (i.e., salience) and top-down attention (Feldman and Friston, 2010; Moran et al., 2013; Kanai et al., 2015)
claims.evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claims.claim: The sudden increase in arousal elicited by cues may correspond to an inflation of expected precision, which would reduce the salience of sensory (exteroceptive) gain in perceptual inference.
claims.source: Thus, the sudden increase in arousal elicited by cues may correspond to an inflation of expected precision, which would reduce the salience of sensory (exteroceptive) gain in perceptual inference.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on theoretical frameworks.

claims.claim: The study does not explicitly manipulate the underlying probability of receiving an arousing cue.
claims.source: However, here we do not explicitly manipulate the underlying probability of receiving an arousing cue.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about a limitation of the current study design.

claims.claim: The study demonstrates a close linkage of perceptual confidence, unexpected arousal, and related interoceptive signals.
claims.source: In the present study, we demonstrate a close linkage of perceptual confidence, unexpected arousal, and related interoceptive signals.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study's findings.

claims.claim: Across perceptual, physiological, and subjective measures the study demonstrates that the encoding of sensory noise is weighted by interoceptive arousal.
claims.source: Across perceptual, physiological, and subjective measures we demonstrate that the encoding of sensory noise is weighted by interoceptive arousal.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study's findings.

claims.claim: The results may have important implications for understanding medical and psychiatric disorders, in which patients exhibit chronic alterations in arousal or interoception.
claims.source: These results may have important implications for understanding medical and psychiatric disorders, in which patients exhibit chronic alterations in arousal or interoception.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential implications of the findings.

claims.claim: Substance abuse, psychosis, anxiety, and depression have been linked to altered heart-rate variability, physiological responses, and interoceptive sensitivity.
claims.source: Substance abuse, psychosis, anxiety, and depression for example have been linked to altered heart-rate variability, physiological responses, and interoceptive sensitivity (Dawson et al., 1977; Hoehn-Saric and McLeod, 2000).
claims.evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claims.claim: The altered psychophysiology of patients with certain disorders may cause them to perceive an unrealistically (un)-certain world.
claims.source: Our results suggest that the altered psychophysiology of these patients may cause them to perceive an unrealistically (un)-certain world.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative implication drawn from the study's findings.

claims.claim: Previous studies examining the impact of sensory noise on confidence have reported samples of 7–20 participants.
claims.source: Previous studies examining the impact of sensory noise on confidence (Zylberberg et al., 2014; Spence et al., 2016) and pupillometric responses during decision making (Murphy et al., 2014b) have reported samples of 7–20 participants.
claims.evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claims.claim: The study recruited a sample of 29 participants to ensure a robust estimate of behavioral and physiological effects while accounting for potential missing data.
claims.source: To ensure a robust estimate of our behavioural and physiological effect while accounting for potential missing data (due to e.g., trials rejected due to blinks), we recruited a larger sample of 29 participants (17 F) aged 18–39 (M = 25.4, SD = 5.0) in total.
claims.evidence: This describes the rationale for the sample size in the study design.

claims.claim: All participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision with no history of neurological or psychiatric disorders.
claims.source: All participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision with no history of neurological or psychiatric disorders.
claims.evidence: This describes the inclusion criteria for participants.

claims.claim: Participants completed 10 blocks of a psychophysical metacognition task consisting of 640 trials divided evenly between four conditions.
claims.source: Participants completed 10 blocks of a psychophysical metacognition task consisting of 640 trials divided evenly between four conditions, with enforced breaks following each 64 trial block.
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claims.claim: At the conclusion of the experiment, participants completed 200 trials of a forced-choice cue-identity detection task to quantify masking efficacy.
claims.source: At the conclusion of the experiment, participants were, (1) asked if they had noticed anything unusual about the presented faces, (2), debriefed that on half the trials there had been a hidden emotional face, and (3) completed 200 trials of a forced-choice cue-identity detection task to quantify masking efficacy.
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claims.claim: Motion stimuli comprised a random dot stimulus moving in an approximately upward-vertical direction presented at 100% coherence.
claims.source: Motion stimuli comprised a random dot stimulus moving in an approximately upward-vertical direction. The stimuli were always presented at 100% coherence, that is, all dots were "signal dots" but the distribution of motion vectors was varied parametrically.
claims.evidence: This describes the stimulus properties in the experimental design.

claims.claim: The mean signal (the average direction of dots) was controlled across trials using an adaptive 2 up 1down staircase which converges on 70.7% accuracy.
claims.source: To control discrimination performance, the mean signal (the average direction of dots) was controlled across trials using an adaptive 2 up 1down staircase which converges on 70.7% accuracy (Cornsweet, 1962; Fleming and Lau, 2014).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental design supported by cited references.

claims.claim: Disgust and neutral trials were thresholded separately to allow for the possibility of the priming condition contributing to detection accuracy.
claims.source: Disgust and neutral trials were thresholded separately to allow for the possibility of the priming condition contributing to detection accuracy (although overall they did not).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental design and a finding that the priming condition did not affect accuracy.

claims.claim: Four paired male faces showing forward-directed disgust or neutral expressions were selected from the Karolinska Directed Emotional Faces database.
claims.source: For emotional face cues, four paired male faces showing forward-directed disgust or neutral expressions were selected from the Karolinska Directed Emotional Faces database (KDEF; Lundqvist et al., 1998)
claims.evidence: This describes the stimulus materials used in the study.

claims.claim: Disgusted faces were selected based on highest mean arousal and intensity scores.
claims.source: Disgusted faces were selected based on highest mean arousal and intensity scores (Goeleven et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This describes the stimulus selection criteria supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The study used a combination of forward and backwards masking to ensure cues were not consciously visible.
claims.source: Following established protocols, we used a combination of forward and backwards masking to ensure cues were not consciously visible (Bachmann and Francis, 2013; Overgaard and Overgaard, 2015).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental procedure supported by cited references.

claims.claim: The monitor was calibrated with a Minolta CS-100A photometer and linearized in software.
claims.source: The monitor was calibrated with a Minolta CS-100A photometer and linearized in software, giving a mean and maximum luminance of 42.5 and 85 cd/m2, respectively.
claims.evidence: This describes the technical procedures for stimulus presentation.

claims.claim: Face stimuli were set to grayscale and pre-processed using the SHINE toolbox in MATLAB, which uses a histogram-matching procedure to balance images both in terms of average luminance and local statistical properties.
claims.source: Face stimuli were set to grayscale and pre-processed using the SHINE toolbox in MATLAB, which uses a histogram-matching procedure to balance images both in terms of average luminance and local statistical properties (Willenbockel et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This describes the stimulus preparation procedure supported by a citation.

claims.claim: ECG signals were measured using disposable Ag/AgCl bipolar surface electrodes affixed just below the left and right clavicle and a ground electrode affixed to the nape of the neck.
claims.source: ECG signals were measured using disposable Ag/AgCl bipolar surface electrodes (100 Foam, Covidien) affixed just below the left and right clavicle and a ground electrode affixed to the nape of the neck using medical tape and Spectra 360 salt-free electrode gel (Parker Laboratories).
claims.evidence: This describes the physiological recording procedure.

claims.claim: ECG signals were amplified using an Asalab System and recorded via Visor2 2.0 software at a 1024 Hz sampling rate.
claims.source: ECG signals were amplified using an Asalab System (ANT Neuro Recording) and recorded via Visor2 2.0 software at a 1024 Hz sampling rate.
claims.evidence: This describes the physiological recording procedure.

claims.claim: Changes in pupil diameter were monitored using an Eyelink 1000 eye tracker recording at 1000 Hz sampling rate.

results.result: The study employed a novel psychophysical paradigm in which 29 participants performed a motion discrimination task where masked disgust or neutral face cues preceded motion stimuli of variable precision. Performance was held constant across conditions using adaptive staircases, and extensive controls were implemented to ensure luminance matching, effective masking, and physiological signal quality.
results.evaluation: The experimental design is well-documented with appropriate controls (C37-C43), successful masking verification (C39, C43), stable performance across blocks (C40), and rigorous physiological recording procedures (C121-C123). The adaptive staircase successfully equated task difficulty across conditions (C36, C38, C40, C41), allowing isolation of confidence effects independent of accuracy.

results.result: Control analyses confirmed that adaptive staircases were stable, successfully controlled for cue-induced differences in detection difficulty, and the masking procedure prevented conscious detection of cue valence. Cues had no effect on motion discrimination sensitivity, reaction times, or thresholds.
results.evaluation: Multiple statistical tests with appropriate significance thresholds support these claims (C40: F(1,24), all p>0.12; C41: all ps>0.1; C43: all 95% CIs span zero). These controls are essential for isolating the effects of arousal on confidence independent of task performance, strengthening the study's internal validity.

results.result: Increased sensory noise (motion variance) slowed reaction times and decreased sensitivity, replicating previous findings. A significant variance × cue interaction was found for response bias, with disgust cues increasing rightward bias specifically for low-variance trials, in the absence of effects on discrimination speed or accuracy.
results.evaluation: The effects are supported by appropriate statistical tests with significant p-values (C44: F(1,24)=4.76, p=0.039; C45: F(1,24)=185.15, p<0.001; C47: F(1,24)=10.46, p=0.004; C49: t(24)=3.76, p<0.001). The replication of previous findings (C44, C45) and the specificity of the bias effect to low-variance trials (C49) support the interpretation that arousal modulates precision-dependent processing.

results.result: Using signal detection theory modeling of confidence, arousing disgust cues counteracted the conservative bias induced by high sensory noise (significant variance × cue interaction on M-Bias), without affecting metacognitive sensitivity (M-Ratio). Following neutral cues, confidence was more conservative for noisy stimuli, but disgust cues eliminated this effect.
results.evaluation: The primary metacognitive finding is supported by significant statistics (C53: F(1,24)=6.19, p=0.020; C54: t(24)=2.25, p=0.034) and appropriate controls showing no effect on M-Ratio (C56: all p>0.6). The dissociation between M-Bias and M-Ratio (C57: r=0.37, p=0.07) supports the interpretation that arousal specifically affects confidence bias rather than metacognitive sensitivity. This is a core finding supporting the interoceptive inference hypothesis.

results.result: Physiological responses showed canonical orientation responses in both pupil and cardiac measures. Sensory noise increased pupil dilation, while confidence showed a biphasic relationship with pupil dilation (positive during stimulus, negative during rating). Disgust cues significantly increased both pupil dilation and cardiac acceleration, and confidence was positively correlated with heart rate acceleration throughout the trial.
results.evaluation: All physiological effects are supported by cluster-corrected permutation tests with significant p-values (C61: cluster p=0.014; C63: cluster p=0.032 for pupil, p=0.044 for cardiac; C64: cluster ps=0.046 and 0.002). The biphasic pupil-confidence relationship (C62) is well-characterized with specific timing parameters. These findings establish that the experimental manipulation successfully modulated arousal and that physiological signals track confidence.

results.result: Pupil responses encoded the interaction of cue and motion variance, with cues reversing the dilatory effect of sensory noise. Critically, this cue-induced reversal of pupillary noise encoding was related to confidence in a significant three-way interaction, demonstrating that trial-by-trial confidence fluctuations tracked the physiological encoding of the arousal-noise interaction.
results.evaluation: The key three-way interaction is supported by significant cluster-corrected statistics (C66: peak 1512ms, cluster p=0.008). This finding directly links the behavioral confidence effects to physiological arousal responses, providing strong evidence for the interoceptive inference mechanism. The temporal specificity (locked to response interval) strengthens the interpretation.

results.result: Cardiac signals were insensitive to sensory noise or noise-by-cue interactions. However, the cue-related cardiac effect negatively interacted with confidence, demonstrating that experimentally induced arousal disrupted the typical positive relationship between heart rate acceleration and confidence.
results.evaluation: The cardiac findings are supported by appropriate statistics (C70: cluster p=0.044). The dissociation between pupil (which encoded noise interactions) and cardiac (which did not) responses is important for understanding the specificity of physiological mechanisms. However, the interpretation remains somewhat uncertain regarding causality (see C87-C88), which the authors appropriately acknowledge.

results.result: The study's primary conclusion is that unexpected arousal regulates perceptual precision, such that subjective confidence reflects the integration of both external sensory and internal embodied states. This integration is consistent with interoceptive inference mechanisms and supports a role for decision-independent sources in guiding confidence.
results.evaluation: This overarching conclusion is well-supported by converging evidence across behavioral (C53-C55), physiological (C65-C67, C70), and correlational (C6, C66) measures. The experimental design successfully isolated arousal effects from task performance (C29, C41-C42), strengthening causal inference. The consistency with interoceptive inference theory (C73, C82) is appropriate given the pattern of results, though alternative models are discussed (C89-C93).

results.result: The study demonstrates consistent correlations between trial-by-trial confidence and interoceptive arousal indexed by both cardiac acceleration and pupil dilation. Pupil dilation showed a biphasic relationship with confidence, and this is the first study to show that perceptual confidence correlates positively with cardiac acceleration.
results.evaluation: The correlational findings are supported by the physiological data (C62, C64) and appropriately contextualized with previous literature (C78). The novelty claim (C79) regarding cardiac-confidence correlation for perception is reasonable given the cited prior work on memory. The biphasic pupil effect (C76) is well-documented and provides insight into distinct computational stages.

results.result: The results are difficult to accommodate within feed-forward observer models that posit confidence depends solely on sensory information. Alternative models (evidence accumulation, two-stage models) could potentially explain some effects but would not predict the observed nonlinear interaction between unexpected arousal and confidence.
results.evaluation: This theoretical evaluation is well-reasoned given the experimental design that isolated arousal from accuracy (C29, C89). The authors appropriately consider alternative computational frameworks (C90-C92) but correctly note that these cannot account for the nonlinear interaction pattern (C93). This strengthens the case for interoceptive inference models while maintaining appropriate scientific caution.

results.result: Disgust cues enhanced rightward bias for high-precision stimuli, which may reflect unconscious arousal strengthening the influence of priors on perceptual inference. This interpretation is consistent with the role of expected precision in attention, where arousal-induced inflation of expected precision could reduce the salience of sensory gain.
results.evaluation: While the response bias effect is empirically supported (C94), the interpretation is largely speculative (C95, C97, C101). The connection to gambler's fallacy (C96) and expected precision mechanisms (C98, C100) is theoretically plausible but not directly tested. The authors appropriately acknowledge this limitation (C102) by noting they did not manipulate arousal probability. This interpretation requires further experimental validation.

results.result: The biphasic pupil-confidence relationship may partially account for findings that distinct stimulus-related and post-decisional computations underlie confidence representation. The results corroborate that pupil variability indexes the impact of unexpected arousal on perceptual precision, consistent with proposals that pupil dilation relates to cortical gain.
results.evaluation: The interpretation linking the biphasic effect to distinct computational stages (C77) is reasonable given the temporal dissociation and is supported by appropriate citations. The connection to cortical gain mechanisms (C84, C85) is well-grounded in prior literature and consistent with the current findings. However, the mechanistic claims remain somewhat inferential.

results.result: While cues shifted the mapping between heart rate and confidence, no influence of sensory noise on cardiac signals was observed. This may reflect either that cardiac effects are downstream of central arousal or that cardiac signals encode interoceptive but not exteroceptive certainty.
results.evaluation: The empirical finding (C86) is supported, but the interpretation remains speculative (C87, C88). The authors appropriately acknowledge this uncertainty and suggest that future pharmacological studies with cardiac-specific manipulations are needed to resolve the causal question. This represents an important limitation in understanding the specific role of cardiac signals.

results.result: The study has potential clinical implications for understanding psychiatric disorders with altered arousal or interoception (substance abuse, psychosis, anxiety, depression), suggesting that altered psychophysiology may cause patients to perceive an unrealistically uncertain or certain world. However, the study did not manipulate arousal probability, limiting conclusions about expected precision.
results.evaluation: The clinical implications (C105, C107) are speculative extrapolations from the current findings. While the link between these disorders and altered psychophysiology is established (C106), the causal claim about perceptual uncertainty (C107) goes beyond the data. The acknowledged limitation (C102) regarding arousal probability manipulation is important for future work but does not undermine the core findings.

results.result: Data preprocessing procedures were appropriate and well-documented, including exclusion of initial trials for staircase stabilization, binning of confidence ratings for signal-theoretic modeling, and rigorous artifact rejection for physiological signals, resulting in reasonable rejection rates (19.3% for pupil, 6.9% for ECG).
results.evaluation: The preprocessing procedures are standard and well-justified (C124-C127, C129). The rejection rates (C128, C130) are reasonable and transparently reported. The use of established software packages (C126: Fieldtrip) and algorithms (C129: Pan-Tomkins) with appropriate citations strengthens reproducibility. These methodological details support the validity of the physiological analyses.

results.result: The study found that arousing disgust cues modulated the encoding of sensory noise across perceptual bias, uncertainty, and physiological arousal measures. Specifically, disgust cues counter-acted the conservative bias induced by high sensory noise, and trial-by-trial pupil fluctuations encoding the nonlinear interaction between arousal and sensory noise correlated with confidence.
results.evaluation: Reviewers raised fundamental concerns about the theoretical interpretation of these findings. They questioned whether the nonlinear hypothesis is necessary, noting that 'the summation hypothesis (2) is sufficiently addressed' and asking 'why arousal cannot boost confidence by linearly offsetting the effects of noise.' The reviewers also challenged the connection to predictive coding, stating 'there's nothing from the current findings that is related to the core concepts of predictive coding – expectations and error representations.' While the data showing effects are not disputed, the mechanistic interpretation is questioned.

results.result: The authors conclude that unexpected arousal regulates perceptual precision, such that subjective confidence reflects the integration of both external sensory and internal, embodied states, consistent with an interoceptive inference mechanism.
results.evaluation: Reviewers expressed significant concerns about the causal interpretation and theoretical grounding. They noted that 'what is being manipulated in the study appears to be physiological arousal, not heart rate or pupil dilation' and that 'the connection between interoception of heart rate and pupil dilation and confidence is correlational.' Reviewers advised the authors to 'focus the conclusions on arousal, rather than interoception of heart rate or pupil dilation.' The theoretical connection to interoceptive inference was also questioned as not well-grounded in the evidence.

results.result: The authors interpret their findings through the lens of cortical gain mechanisms, suggesting that precision is encoded by the gain of local pyramidal cells regulated by neuromodulators, and that pupil variability indexes the impact of unexpected arousal on perceptual precision.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly challenged the use of 'gain' concepts, stating 'what does cortical gain and sensory gain mean exactly in these contexts, in what fashion are they modulated by the experimental manipulations, and how exactly they produce the effects that the authors attribute to them, are unclear.' They noted that 'Gain is a term that simply describes changes in the power of signals. It does not have the non-linearity or other complex properties that the authors seemed to be using to explain their findings.' Reviewers also expressed concerns about 'the connection to locus coeruleus and particular neurotransmitters,' noting 'we do not have an understanding of the locus coeruleus that allows us to directly link pupil dilation to a certain neurotransmitter.'

results.result: Unseen disgust cues successfully modulated arousal, as evidenced by significant increases in both pupil dilation and cardiac acceleration.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledged that 'the findings, showing that physiological arousal, as reflected by changes in pupil sizes and heart rate, influences judgment of perceptual confidence' were demonstrated. The manipulation check showing arousal modulation was not questioned, though reviewers clarified that arousal itself, not the physiological measures, was the manipulated variable.

results.result: Control analyses confirmed that staircases were stable, successfully controlled for cue-induced differences in detection difficulty, the masking procedure prevented detection of cue valence, and cues did not affect motion discrimination sensitivity, reaction times, or motion thresholds.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not raise concerns about these methodological controls. The experimental design was described as 'carefully designed' and these control measures were not questioned, indicating implicit acceptance of their validity.

results.result: The study demonstrated correlations between trial-by-trial confidence and interoceptive arousal indexed by cardiac acceleration and pupil dilation, with pupil dilation showing a biphasic relationship with confidence and the study being the first to show positive correlation between perceptual confidence and cardiac acceleration.
results.evaluation: While reviewers did not dispute the correlational findings, they emphasized that 'the connection between interoception of heart rate and pupil dilation and confidence is correlational' and that 'the causal relationship that the results seem to support is one between arousal and confidence, not heart rate/pupil and confidence.' This indicates the correlations are accepted but their interpretation as reflecting interoceptive mechanisms is questioned.

results.result: The authors argue their results are difficult to accommodate within feed-forward observer models and that alternative models like evidence accumulation or two-stage models would not predict the observed nonlinear interaction.
results.evaluation: Reviewers questioned the necessity of the nonlinear hypothesis and the dismissal of simpler alternatives. They noted that 'the necessity for something complex, i.e. the non-linear hypothesis illustrated in Figure 1, is questionable' and asked 'why arousal cannot boost confidence by linearly offsetting the effects of noise.' The reviewers also questioned how adaptive gain theory 'would produce a non-linearity' and noted it 'does not seem to be compatible with the authors' finding that perceptual performance is not enhanced by physiological arousal.'

results.result: Increased sensory noise rendered motion discrimination more difficult, slowing reaction times and decreasing sensitivity, and following neutral cues, confidence reports were more conservative for noisy stimuli, replicating previous findings.
results.evaluation: These replication findings were not questioned by reviewers and represent standard effects in the field that serve as validation of the experimental paradigm.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on methodological controls (C37-C43). Both evaluations find these experimental controls SUPPORTED. OpenEval provides detailed statistical validation while peer reviewers implicitly accept the 'carefully designed' experimental approach without raising concerns.

Strong disagreement on theoretical interpretation (C89-C93). OpenEval finds the dismissal of linear alternatives and support for nonlinear interoceptive inference SUPPORTED, while peer reviewers rate this UNCERTAIN, questioning 'why arousal cannot boost confidence by linearly offsetting the effects of noise' and challenging the necessity of complex nonlinear models.

Major disagreement on overarching conclusions (C5-C8, C72-C74, C80, C103-C104). OpenEval finds the interoceptive inference interpretation SUPPORTED with converging evidence, while peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, arguing that 'what is being manipulated...appears to be physiological arousal, not heart rate or pupil dilation' and that the interoceptive connection is merely correlational.

Fundamental disagreement on core theoretical claims (C5-C6, C82). OpenEval supports the interoceptive inference framework, while peer reviewers question whether 'the nonlinear hypothesis is necessary' and state 'there's nothing from the current findings that is related to the core concepts of predictive coding.' Both address the same central claims but reach opposite conclusions about theoretical grounding.

Disagreement on three-way interaction interpretation (C65-C68). OpenEval finds this SUPPORTED as 'strong evidence for the interoceptive inference mechanism,' while peer reviewers rate the broader theoretical interpretation UNCERTAIN, questioning the predictive coding connection and mechanistic claims.

Partial disagreement on metacognitive findings (C53-C58). OpenEval finds the M-Bias effects SUPPORTED as core evidence for interoceptive inference, while peer reviewers accept the empirical findings but question the theoretical interpretation, rating the broader claims UNCERTAIN.

Disagreement on correlational findings interpretation (C75-C76, C79). OpenEval finds these SUPPORTED and appropriately contextualized, while peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, emphasizing that 'the connection between interoception of heart rate and pupil dilation and confidence is correlational' and questioning causal claims about interoceptive mechanisms.

Partial overlap on physiological correlations (C62, C64). OpenEval finds all physiological effects SUPPORTED with appropriate statistics, while peer reviewers accept the correlations but emphasize they are correlational rather than causal evidence for interoception.

Agreement on arousal manipulation (C63). Both evaluations accept that physiological arousal was successfully modulated. OpenEval rates SUPPORTED with cluster-corrected statistics, peer reviewers also rate SUPPORTED, acknowledging 'physiological arousal, as reflected by changes in pupil sizes and heart rate, influences judgment of perceptual confidence.'

Strong disagreement on gain mechanisms (C84-C85). OpenEval finds the cortical gain interpretation SUPPORTED and 'well-grounded in prior literature,' while peer reviewers rate UNSUPPORTED, stating 'what does cortical gain and sensory gain mean exactly...are unclear' and that 'Gain is a term that simply describes changes in the power of signals' without the complex properties claimed.

Agreement on basic behavioral effects (C44-C45). Both evaluations accept these replication findings as SUPPORTED. OpenEval provides statistical validation while peer reviewers implicitly accept these as standard effects validating the experimental paradigm.

Agreement on M-Bias empirical finding (C54). Both accept the statistical result showing arousal effects on confidence bias, though peer reviewers question the broader theoretical interpretation in other results.

OpenEval finds experimental design and methodological procedures (C4, C30-C36, C109-C123) SUPPORTED with detailed validation of controls, masking, and physiological recording. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses these methodological details, though they are implicitly accepted.

OpenEval finds arousal effects on behavior (C44-C50) SUPPORTED with significant statistics and appropriate interpretation of precision-dependent processing. Peer reviewers address some overlapping claims (C44-C45) but do not specifically evaluate the full set of behavioral effects and their interpretation.

OpenEval finds cardiac findings (C69-C71) SUPPORTED but acknowledges uncertainty about causality. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses the cardiac dissociation from pupil effects, though broader concerns about causal interpretation appear in other peer results.

OpenEval rates response bias interpretation (C94-C101) as UNCERTAIN, noting the connection to gambler's fallacy and expected precision is speculative and not directly tested. No corresponding peer review evaluation addresses these specific claims about response bias mechanisms.

OpenEval rates cardiac mechanism interpretation (C86-C88) as UNCERTAIN, acknowledging the causal question requires future pharmacological studies. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses the cardiac-specific mechanistic claims.

OpenEval rates clinical implications (C102, C105-C107) as UNCERTAIN, noting these are speculative extrapolations beyond the data. No corresponding peer review evaluation addresses the clinical implications or limitations regarding arousal probability manipulation.

OpenEval finds preprocessing procedures (C124-C130) SUPPORTED as standard, well-justified, and appropriately documented. No corresponding peer review evaluation addresses these technical preprocessing details.

Peer reviewers rate gain mechanism claims (C24-C25, C99) as UNSUPPORTED, challenging the conceptual clarity and mechanistic specificity of 'cortical gain' and 'sensory gain,' and questioning connections to locus coeruleus and neurotransmitters. OpenEval addresses some overlapping claims (C84-C85) in R12 but does not evaluate C24-C25 or C99 specifically.
